paragraphs: On the day she left Wanyan Chi, Qianli Xun wandered the streets of Yanjing alone, turning the question over in her mind: should she leave the city, or go somewhere else? One thing she knew for certain—she would not go back to Lin'an, and she would not go to Bianliang.

Either of those two places would have suited her fine. But after what Wanyan Chi had done to her, she had no courage left to face the person she wanted to see. In the end she decided to stay in Yanjing, on her own.

She had not a coin to her name. She had walked out of the princely manor with nothing. How was she supposed to make a living in Yanjing? She thought about her fists and feet. She would sell her skill, earn a few coins, then rent a roof over her head.

She picked an open patch of ground by the roadside, took off her cloak, folded it neatly on a stone at the foot of the wall, and called out to everyone passing by, "Southbound! Northbound! Look over here!..."
A few people out shopping were drawn in and came closer.
"This girl is new in town and flat broke, but I know a thing or two about fists and feet. I'll perform a set of punches for you. If you like it, toss me a few coins. If not, you owe me nothing."
The crowd grew. Everyone wanted to see what a pretty young thing could do with her fists.

Qianli Xun set her stance. She had created this form of boxing to go with Zhu Shuzhen's lyric "Nian Nu Jiao—Clear Winter, No Snow." She chanted the lines as she struck, each move fitted to a line of the poem. Her voice carried the ache in the words while her fists answered it, hard and soft woven together. It was lovely to watch, and the skill behind it left the onlookers gaping.

When the last line died away, the last punch landed, and the crowd burst into applause. Qianli Xun cupped her hands and went among them for coins. One coin, two coins, dropped into her palms. By the time she had made the rounds she held a decent little handful—enough for a bed tonight.
She was still smiling when Lu Yuanfeng came up and scattered the crowd. "Clear off, all of you. No more show."
The people drifted away.
Qianli Xun cupped her coins and rounded on him. "Lu Yuanfeng! How dare you? These were my customers!"
He turned to face her. "Master, who are you? You can't be doing this in the street."
"I'm nobody. Why can't I perform? I'm not breaking my conscience and I'm not breaking the law. Since when is that your business?"

He saw how hard she had worked for those few coins, went to a nearby stall, bought a purse, and began sweeping the money off her palms into it. "Why do this to yourself, Master? Life with the young prince is good. Instead you run out here to perform in the street. If he found out, it would cut him to the heart."
"Did Wanyan Chi send you?"
He finished tucking away the last coin. "Nothing to do with the prince. I was out on an errand, saw you performing, and came over to talk you out of it."
She took the purse back from his hand. "If it has nothing to do with him, fine. Save your breath. Don't tell Wanyan Chi a word about me."

Lu Yuanfeng put on an innocent face. "I don't want to get in the middle of what's between you two. But I will say this much for him: I've been at his side a good while, and he's never fussed over a girl the way he fusses over you."

"So what? Plenty of people have been good to me. Am I supposed to love every one of them? A man who forces himself on a woman and calls it love—that's the sort I despise most. He waves a flag of affection while using brute force, and it's nothing but his own appetite. Don't think I'm blind. I see straight through it."
Lu Yuanfeng gave her a thumbs-up. "You're a heroine among women, Master. Nothing like the rest. I admire you."
"Don't butter me up." She tucked the purse away, went back to the stone, picked up her cloak, put it on, and made to leave.
He stepped in front of her. "Master, are you leaving Yanjing?"
"What business is it of yours? Get out of my way." She sidestepped him.
He called after her. "Master! If you're staying in Yanjing, I can find you a place to live!"
She had been worrying about exactly that, so she stopped and turned. "You swear Wanyan Chi didn't send you?"
He kept up the lie. "He didn't, I swear. I call you Master. I can't stand by and watch you end up on the streets. Lending a hand is only right."

"Where is this place? Take me there." Her tone softened. She needed a roof badly, and here was one handed to her; she might as well take it. Even if Wanyan Chi were behind it, she wasn't afraid. If he dared show his face, one of them would not walk away.
Glad she had relented, Lu Yuanfeng said, "Not far off. There's an empty room in a lane nearby. Perfect for you."
Qianli Xun eyed him. "You live in the manor with Wanyan Chi day and night. How do you come to have a room out here?"
He gave a sly little laugh. "I'm a man. A man likes to keep a woman or two, and that's awkward in the manor. I rented this place, but she hasn't moved in yet. You can have it first."
"Am I ruining your little arrangement?"
"Don't say that. It's an honor to have you there."
She pulled out the purse, walked up, and held it out to him. "Rent for tonight. It's not much, don't mind that. Once I'm settled and earning more silver, I'll make it up to you."
He pushed her hand back. "How could I take rent from you, Master? Settle in and don't worry."
"If you won't take it, I won't stay."
"All right, all right, I'll take it." He thought for a moment. "But you need money to live on. Keep your coins. Pay me later, when you've earned more."
That made sense to her, so she took the purse back. "Thanks. Lead the way."
The room Lu Yuanfeng had rented was nothing fancy, but for someone who needed a place to lay her head it was more than good enough. She settled in with an easy mind.

Later, saying she needed to pay off the rent quickly, he found her work writing letters for people and supplying new poems for a teahouse, for the tea drinkers to enjoy. It came to a tael of silver a month. Not much, but enough to put her mind at rest.

She had not forgotten her huaben, either. Storytelling was banned in Yanjing, though. After a fair bit of hunting she found a storyteller and gave him the manuscript for free, saying the writer Qianli Xun had left it with her for him. He was delighted when he read it and promised to find a way to send the huaben out of the city.
So that the people might hear the huaben she wrote afterward, she told him the writer Qianli Xun would be supplying more.
The storyteller said eagerly, "I'm the only one in Yanjing with a way to get huaben out. Bring me every one you have. I'll take as many as you can carry."
She agreed gladly.
The Song had entered the first year of Jingkang—a year of shame waiting just around the corner.

New Year's Day came and she spent it in a strange land, aching for her family and the man she loved. She supposed they all thought her dead. She had no wish to go back and disturb the quiet lives they had built.

On the sixth night of the first month the sky was clear and a new moon rose. Qianli Xun wrapped her cloak around her and went into the yard. She tipped her face up to the crescent, thinking of old friends, and of the Divine Willow she used to go and see.

The sorrow of the age weighed heavier on her in a foreign place. Tomorrow she was due to deliver poems to the teahouse, and the owner had asked her not to write anything too sad during the festival—but all she could remember were sad lines.

Just as she was stuck, she remembered it was the sixth of the first month, and that Zhu Shuzhen had a lyric called "Yi Qin E—The Moon on the Sixth Night of the First Month," which fitted the night and would please the teahouse besides. She went inside, took up her brush, and wrote:
Crooked, crooked, the new moon of the new year, a hook of cold jade. A hook of cold jade, small phoenix shoes, eyebrows gathered green.
Hairpins like moths and willows of snow add to her dress; candle-dragon and fire-tree race and chase. Race and chase—the Lantern Festival on the fifteenth cannot match this sixth day.
When she came to the signature she hesitated. The Jin had ordered everyone to use their reign title; to refuse was punishable by death.

She hesitated a moment, then wrote firmly, "First year of Jingkang, sixth day of the first month." She would not use the Jin calendar. Let them put her to the sword if they must. Everyone she loved believed her dead already.
Nothing happened. The poems went up in the teahouse as usual. She guessed Lu Yuanfeng had smoothed the way—he was doing well for himself at Wanyan Chi's side, after all.

Spring made life easier for her. To her relief Wanyan Chi left her in peace, and she believed more strongly than ever what Lu Yuanfeng had said: everything he had done had nothing to do with the prince.
Just as the peach blossoms opened, Lu Yuanfeng brought her another job: teaching Jin children to read and write Chinese.

At first she refused. Then she thought it over. Learning Chinese culture was the best way to make the Jin more Chinese. How many Han people had their wars hurt? Here was her chance to win their children over, to make them think as Han people thought.
She was pleased with the plan. When Lu Yuanfeng came again, she told him she would take the job.
The outer room of her house became a schoolroom. Six Jin children came each day. To reshape their minds, she pored day and night over the books she had bought.
Her teaching bore fruit. All six came to believe that Jin and Han were one family, and that they should never make war and kill one another.
That day she was teaching the children the Analects when Lu Yuanfeng came running in and sat down at the side to listen a while.
After the children left, she brought him a bag of silver. "Thank you for all your help. A year's rent is covered. Take it."
He accepted with a show of reluctance. "What are your plans for today, Master?"
"A strange question. What plans could I have? I go shopping at this hour every day. My brush has been shedding hairs for ages and the ink stick is nearly gone. It's time I bought more."

He was uneasy at the thought of her going to the main street. If she ran into the Prince Yi, or heard people talking, it could wreck the young prince's scheme. "I know a shop with very good brushes and ink," he suggested. "Let me take you there."
She thought nothing of it. "If you recommend it, it must be good. Wait outside a moment. I'll change my clothes and come."
While she was changing, he went to the cabinet, pulled open a drawer, put the bag of silver inside, and murmured to himself, "The prince paid the rent. How could I take your silver?"
When she had changed, she went shopping with him.
He led her along back streets, where there were few people and few shops. She grew suspicious. "Why are you taking me into the back lanes? We haven't passed a single shop selling brushes and ink."
"Patience. It's just ahead." He took the chance to add, "Master, I'd like to stay with you from now on."
She walked on. "No need. Go and keep company with that woman you're secretly keeping."
"What woman could matter more than you, Master? I'll stay with you."
Worried he had designs on her, she stopped short. "What do you mean?"
He read her face and saw he had gone too far. "Don't take me wrong, Master. How would I dare want the woman the young prince loves? I only respect you."
She let out a breath and walked on. "Don't mention him in front of me again."
"You haven't said whether you'll let me come with you."
"No! I'm used to being on my own these days!"
He hurried after her. They turned a corner and at last came to a shop selling brushes and ink. Lucky the stock was good, or his story would have fallen apart then and there.

Meanwhile Wanyan Chi had led his men to the gate of Yanjing and climbed the high wall to look down. Jin soldiers had stopped and scattered the townspeople coming and going; the gate was ringed with them inside and out.
Standing below the wall, Shen Jianchen glared up at him. "Why are you here alone? Where is the person I asked for?"
Wanyan Chi lied again. "I told you last year. She's dead."
Shen Jianchen would not be fooled a second time. "Your lies won't work on me. If you haven't brought the person I want, don't expect to see the one you want."
Wanyan Chi's eyes went to the two carriages. "Is the person I want in one of those?"
Shen Jianchen pointed. "She's in that one."
Tears of relief ran down Wanyan Chi's face. When he had himself a little under control, he asked, "How do I know you're not deceiving me?"
A woman's voice came from the carriage. "Prince Yi, come here."
The voice was kind and gentle. Even from where he stood high on the wall, Wanyan Chi caught enough of it to know it was exactly the voice of the mother he had imagined.
The Prince Yi of Great Song walked to the carriage. Someone inside seemed to say something to him. He cupped his hands in a bow, then raised his head and looked up.
"The person the young prince wants to see tells me you have a red mole behind your left ear. Is that true?"
Wanyan Chi's last defenses gave way. He ran down the wall steps, rushed through the gate, and reached the carriage in tears.
"Are you my mother?..."
Inside, Shao Yueting was weeping too. "I am your own mother..."
Wanyan Chi fell to his knees. "Mother, I searched so hard for you! Why did you hide and never let me find you?"
"What good would finding me do? It would only bring more sorrow."
"Mother, come down. Let me look at you properly."
"I came today to save a life. Until you set that girl free, I will not step down from this carriage."
"All right. I'll free her. If I can see you, there's nothing I won't do."
With Wanyan Chi agreeing, Shen Jianchen could hardly contain his joy. "Where is she?"
He lied again. "She's at the manor. Once I've seen my mother, I'll let her go. But you must grant me one condition."
Shen Jianchen asked cautiously, "What condition?"
"I'll keep my word and send her back to Lin'an. But you must stay in Yanjing for a year and teach me and my master everything you know of boxing. And when she leaves, you are not to see her off."
Shen Jianchen did not trust him. "You dare make demands of me? Are you not afraid I'll simply turn back?"
"Open your eyes. My men are everywhere. You can't escape."

Shen Jianchen had seen the soldiers. He had expected bringing Shao Yueting here would win Qianli Xun back without trouble, and that he and she would go home to Lin'an together. He had not taken the surrounding Jin troops seriously.

Now he saw the prince was full of tricks and meant to keep him here to learn boxing. If it came to a fight, he could not win alone, and things would only get worse—he might lose Qianli Xun and himself as well. A year, then. A year would also give him the chance to find out where Shen Fist had come from.
"You must promise to send her back to Lin'an in good faith. No tricks."
"What is most precious to me is already mine. I dare not ask for more. She doesn't want me, so I'll set her free and let her go to the man she loves."
Shao Yueting's voice came from the carriage again. "If you deceive Prince Yi, I will never step down to see you."
"Mother, I mean it. Come home to the manor with me. Once I've laid eyes on you, I'll let her go."
"Very well. I'll go with you to the manor."
Inside the manor Wanyan Chi finally saw his mother. She sat upright in a chair, dressed as a nun, Buddhist beads in her hands, her eyes wet.

He knelt before her again. "Mother, no wonder I couldn't find you. You had become a nun. Now that you've found your son, why not return to secular life? Live in Yanjing with me, or go back to Huining?"

Shao Yueting had often wondered what her son would look like, if he were still alive. Every time she saw a young gentleman of about his age among the pilgrims at the convent, she let her mind run. Now she saw her own son in the flesh, taller and broader than she had imagined, his features sharply cut, his nose high—only his skin was dark.
"Come closer. Let me look at you properly."
He shuffled forward on his knees and lifted his face, studying his mother's looks and expression as if he would carve them into his heart.
Standing to one side, Shen Jianchen was moved by the sight. Much as he disliked Wanyan Chi, he had to admit that a grown man seeing his mother for the first time was a pitiful thing.
Shao Yueting touched his face. "So this is what my boy grew up to look like..."
Wanyan Chi pressed his question. "Will you stay, Mother?"
"I have taken vows. Having seen you, I must go back to the convent."
"Did you become a nun because you didn't want to see me?"
"What mother doesn't want to see her son? I thought you were gone from this world, and your father was dead too. I saw no point in staying among the living, so I became a nun."
"It must be Shao Zhengye who lied to you."
Her heart went out to him. "Get up. Sit and talk with me."
He stood, told a maid to bring a chair, and sat beside his mother. Once seated, he kept hold of her hand.
"Don't blame your uncle. Blame me. I was young and foolish, and I loved someone I should never have loved..."
"Do you regret meeting His Majesty, Mother?"
"I did once. Now the clouds have cleared."
"If His Majesty saw you, he would be overjoyed."
"Promise me you won't tell him you found me. I want to live out my days in peace."
He nodded. "All right. But you must spend more time with your son first."
"Very well. I'll stay half a month, then go back to Lin'an."

Wanyan Chi was in high spirits. He turned to Prince Yi standing nearby. "There's paper and ink on the table. Write her a letter, and tell her to leave Yanjing today and never come back to stir up trouble."

It was clear he meant to let her go. Shen Jianchen went to the table without a word and took up the brush. He had no heart left for the mother and son pouring out their feelings to each other; he was thinking over what Wanyan Chi had just said.

If Qianli Xun heard that the prince had kept him here, she might refuse to leave for fear of his safety—she might even come to blows with Wanyan Chi. He did not want to see that, and neither did Wanyan Chi. He had won her back with difficulty; he could not bear for harm to come to her again. He would write and persuade her to go quietly back to Lin'an and wait for him.

Having settled on the words, he set brush to paper. He wrote no form of address, because the name everyone knew was not the person in his heart, and the name he called her in his heart was a secret between the two of them.
At the end he wrote only the character "Shen"—and she alone would know what it meant.
When he had finished, the maid stepped forward and took the letter.
Wanyan Chi called the maid close and whispered a few words in her ear. She only nodded and nodded.
Shen Jianchen said warily, "Wanyan Chi, no tricks."
He laughed. "With my mother here, how could I play tricks? Rest easy. All I want now is to see you two together."
There was sincerity in his face, and Shen Jianchen felt easier.
Qianli Xun had just bought brush and ink and returned to her room when the manor maid came and handed the letter to Lu Yuanfeng.
She recognized the maid. "Lu Yuanfeng, have you been lying to me all along?"
He confessed. "The young prince did send me to help you. He told me to rent this room, and he found you the work that earns your keep too. I'm only the errand boy."
She threw a punch at him. "I'll teach you to lie!"
He dodged. "Don't be angry, Master. The maid has brought a letter from Prince Yi. You'll be glad when you read it."
Her fist faltered and she drew it back. "What? A letter from Prince Yi? Doesn't he think I'm dead? Why would he write to me?"
"I don't know the reason. You'll understand when you've read it." He held the letter out.
She took it, opened it, and read it closely...

Wanyan Chi and Cai Jing told me you were gone from this world. I rushed back to Lin'an and stood beneath the Divine Willow, hoping it would bring you back to me. Then a monk showed me the way: I dragged out a few more days in Lin'an, and heaven took pity. I heard that the scholar Qianli Xun had written a new story, and that Youqi Jushi had new poems—and so I knew you were alive. I brought Wanyan Chi's mother, Shao Yueting, to Yanjing, hoping to trade her for you...
Qianli Xun said under her breath, "How could you be so foolish? I wasn't even at the manor, and you went to all that trouble to save me."

After seeing his own mother, Wanyan Chi promised to let you return to Lin'an, and I am glad. His boxing is rooted in Shen Fist, so I must stay in Yanjing a year and exchange techniques with his master. Forgive me that I could not see you when you left...
Moved and angry at once, she cried, "This has to be one of Wanyan Chi's plots. I'm going to find him now and settle the score!"
Lu Yuanfeng warned her. "Don't fly off the handle yet, Master. Finish the letter before you decide."
She steadied herself and read on.

Once out of Yanjing, don't look back. Don't go looking for a fight with Wanyan Chi. I went to a lot of trouble to get you out; I don't want anything to happen to you. If you have any feeling for me, go back to Lin'an like a good girl and wait for me in our bamboo house. I promise I'll come back to you in one piece a year from now.

I've buried Mengrong and Xilan outside Yanjing. Leave the city and keep going east, and you'll find their graves. Their names are carved on the stones; you can't miss them. Move their remains back to Lin'an for me. The burial place is ready; Bai Feng knows all about it...
Her eyes brimmed. She had come to Yanjing to find a doctor for Mengrong, and Yanjing had become the place where Mengrong was buried.
She glared at Lu Yuanfeng. "Did the Jin kill Mengrong and Xilan?"
He knew nothing about it. "I don't even know who they were. How would I know?"
"If you still admit you're a subject of Great Song, if you still call me your master, find the people who killed them. I want revenge for them."
"That's not hard. Tell me when they died and where, so I can look into it."

She thought it through. It must have been the day the Jin soldiers entered Yanjing. "It should be around the time I first met you last year. They ran off through an alley; they must have been killed there. Ask which band of men went into that alley that day and you'll find them."
The band that went into the alley had been the young prince's own men, Lu Yuanfeng thought; that should make them easy to find. But he would need the prince's permission first.

"The maid who came just now says the young prince wants you out of the city as soon as possible. If you're still inside at nightfall, he won't let you leave. Watch the time. I'll go find those men now and bring them outside the city for you to deal with however you see fit."
When he had gone she went on reading.

You needn't torture yourself any longer over the marriage to Chen Haoyu. In Bianliang His Majesty issued an edict betrothing you to me. Chen Haoyu was unwilling, but the imperial will cannot be disobeyed, and for his family's sake he had to call it off. I was glad, but I would not force you to be mine. I promised him I would never tell you the truth, and that when you came out of prison I would respect your choice...
Now she understood why the two of them had asked her the same question.

Good news for you: the Chen family bought Xiangrong's freedom and put her at Chen Haoyu's side. Before I left for Yanjing I heard he was about to become a father. He has someone now; you needn't worry about him. My efforts have moved heaven at last. You and I can be together with nothing in our way. Remember, do nothing—go back to Lin'an and wait for me.
She stared at the character "Shen" at the foot of the letter. "All right. I'll do as you say. I'll go back and wait for you in the bamboo house."
She folded the letter away and began to pack—a few clothes, her manuscripts, and what little silver she had left.
She opened the drawer to take the silver and found the bag she had paid as rent sitting there, right where it belonged. Lu Yuanfeng must have put it back.

"Fine. Wanyan Chi owes me far too much; even his life couldn't pay it off, and a paltry bag of silver is nothing." She picked up the bag and thought again of what he had done to her. "The virtue I fought so hard to keep went to the dogs. Will you still want me?... We've finally found our way to each other. Why am I filling my head with this? Better get out of the city."
She reached the outskirts and searched a long while before she found where Mengrong was buried.
Tears stood in her eyes. "Mengrong, it's all my fault. If I hadn't insisted on bringing you to Yanjing to see a miracle doctor, you wouldn't have left so soon. Ohhh..."
She cried for a while, then went on. "Today I'm taking you back to Lin'an with me..."
"With no tools and no preparation, how do you plan to dig up the bones and carry them to Lin'an? You're talking through your teeth."
Wanyan Chi's voice came from behind her. She spun around and saw him with a Jin man in custody and several others carrying tools following him.
"What are you doing here?"
"Helping you." He shoved the prisoner toward the grave. "This is the one who hounded your friend to death. I've brought him for you to do with as you please."
She got to her feet, unbelieving. "You'd be that kind?"

"Of course I wouldn't. If I trusted the man, I'd never put him in front of you. The truth is he killed one of my officers, so he has to die. I'm using the chance to do you a favor. Pity I couldn't find the one who killed your maid."
"Hah! I knew you weren't that kind."
"Less talk. Get on with it."

She clenched her fists. "Mengrong, today I avenge you." She threw a punch at the Jin man, but she could not land it. Her fist stopped in midair. She had never struck someone who could not fight back, and she found she did not know how.
The bound man begged for mercy. "Spare me, miss! Spare me, young prince!"
Wanyan Chi struck him on the temple with one punch and he died on the spot. He drew back his fist. "I helped you. Aren't you going to thank me?"
She gave a cold laugh and said nothing.
He called to the men with tools. "Get to work!"
They began breaking open the grave and lifting out the bones. She walked off to one side and waited patiently.
He tried to edge closer to the beauty. She turned her head, too bored to look at him. He did not mind. "Remember, I let you go because I love you and want you to be happy."
She sneered. "Save your sweet talk for someone else. I don't buy it. And listen: send Prince Yi back to Lin'an in a year, safe and sound, or I'll never let you rest for the rest of my days!"
"I'd like that. Then we'd have a reason to cross paths always."
"All right, don't get angry. I promise I'll hand Prince Yi back to you in a year."
"You're a vile piece of work. I'd already left the manor, and you still cooked up a plot to fool him?"

"Prince Yi is clever enough, except where you're concerned. There he turns so stupid he doesn't know it. A small trick from me and he believed it. Don't worry, though. All I want is to trade punches with him, nothing more."
"You wouldn't dare."
The teasing left his face and he turned serious. "Once you're gone, who knows whether we'll ever see each other again?"
"Better never."
"My mother has become a nun and won't stay at my side. I'll go to Lin'an to see her when I can. If I come to Lin'an, will you drink tea with me, as friends?"
She was silent a moment, then said evenly, "I don't want to remember unpleasant things."
He understood the refusal and said, disappointed, "Very well. I won't trouble you again."
He wanted one last embrace, but at the wary look in her eyes he gave it up. "A carriage is ready for you at the crossroads ahead."
He took one last look at her, wistful and tender, then turned and left.
She felt not a grain of gratitude for anything he had done. All she wanted was for him never to appear before her again.
Wanyan Chi went back to the manor and came to a house with heavy guards posted outside.
The guards at the door saw the young prince coming and opened the big lock themselves.
He pushed the door open. Shen Jianchen was sitting at a table, drinking at his ease. He walked over and sat down opposite him.
"I've arranged everything for you as you asked. You can settle in without worry."
"The men outside—is that how you treat a guest?"
"Your boxing is better than mine and my master's. I was afraid you might run."
"Our styles come from the same root. I'm here of my own accord."
"A man's heart is hard to read. Better be careful."
"When do we start trading techniques?"
"Master says tomorrow."
"Good. Tomorrow, then."
Shen Jianchen was calm and unruffled, and he had stolen the beauty's heart besides. It needled Wanyan Chi. He decided to provoke him. "There's something you may not know."
Shen Jianchen did not rise to it and went on drinking. "What?"
Wanyan Chi said shamelessly, "I was her first man."
Shen Jianchen threw the rest of his wine into Wanyan Chi's face.
He laughed. "Ho, ho! What? Regret all that trouble because you can't be her first?"
Shen Jianchen answered with a punch. Wanyan Chi dodged and punched back. They traded several rounds and he began to lose ground.
Unable to win with fists, he went back to words. "So you do regret. From now on, don't make a show of how much you love her in front of me."

Shen Jianchen knocked him down with one punch. "Not regret. Pain. Pain that you and Cai Jing fooled me and I didn't save her in time, so you could ruin her. She must have been so frightened. You're a beast! You don't deserve to love her!"
The corner of Wanyan Chi's mouth split and blood ran down. He wiped it away. "I touched her because I love her. Other women want me to touch them and I can't be bothered."
Shen Jianchen hit him in the face again. "She's mine. Touch her again and I'll kill you."
Wanyan Chi staggered back, grinning through the pain. "I won't touch her again. Being her first is enough for me. Pity you never can be. Ho, ho!"
Shen Jianchen kicked him down and grabbed his collar. "Let me tell you something. I don't care. Stop using this to rile me. Say it once more and I'll send you to your grave."
At last Wanyan Chi said what was in his heart. "That's what I wanted to hear. I'm giving her back to you. Promise me you'll treat her well."
Shen Jianchen shoved him aside and stood. "I don't need you to tell me that."
Wanyan Chi lay on the floor laughing. "Ha, ha, ha..."
When the bones of Mengrong and Xilan were sealed in their coffins, Qianli Xun set out for Lin'an that same night.
The journey went smoothly enough, though there were more people wandering the roads than two-odd years before.
In the war between Song and Jin, common folk suffered most. They lost their homes, and the little property they had scraped together over years.

Set beside those wanderers, Qianli Xun felt her own troubles amounted to nothing. There was no point clinging to what she had lost. She had to look forward; the future that truly belonged to her was waiting.

They traveled north to south through many strange places. She would likely never get another chance to see such country, so she made a point of slowing down. At every stop she halted the carriage and told the red wooden chest in the one behind her what she saw.
In the red chest lay Mengrong's bones. The gray one held Xilan.

While she was alive, her brother fell ill and she stayed at the Prince Yi's manor to nurse him, never getting a chance outside the gates. Later he came back to life—but it was not her real brother. His heart belonged to someone else, and he pushed her aside.
Now that she had the chance, Qianli Xun wanted to use her own eyes to show Mengrong what the wide world looked like.
They went and stopped, going and stopping. A journey of one month took a full month and a half before they reached the borders of Lin'an.
She was in no hurry to enter the city. She told the driver to go first to the bamboo grove.
At the grove the carriage could not go into the village, so they stopped outside it.
As she stepped down, who should she meet but Kujue, on her way out.

Kujue recognized her mistress at a glance but could hardly believe it. She came closer to look, and cried out, "It really is you, mistress! You're alive! If my sister knew, she'd be over the moon! I—I'll run into the city and tell her this minute!"
Qianli Xun caught her arm. "Take me to Prince Yi's bamboo house first."
Kujue was embarrassed. "I was so taken up with my sister I forgot all about you. Let me settle you first, then go to the city."
Guided by Kujue, she came to the bamboo house Shen Jianchen had built.
It stood deep in the village and took up a large plot—the grandest bamboo house in the place. The main hall and side rooms enclosed the whole courtyard, making it feel like a proper manor.
Qianli Xun asked herself, "How did you know I wanted a house like this?"
As they entered the yard, Kujue called out excitedly, "Brother-in-law! Look who's come back!"
Bai Feng came out of a side room. Seeing Youqi Jushi standing before him in the flesh, he was overcome, and bowed to her. "You're back, Youqi Jushi. At last the prince can rest easy."
No prince in sight. Bai Feng asked, "Why didn't His Highness come back with you?"
"Prince Yi... Prince Yi is staying on in Yanjing for a time. He can come home after a year."
Bai Feng worried about the prince but did not press her. He could guess without being told: the prince had stayed only to win Youqi Jushi back.
"The bamboo house was built for you by His Highness. This is your home from now on. You've had a hard journey; come in and rest."
"Not yet. Mengrong's and Xilan's bones are at the village entrance. Let me bury them before I rest."
Bai Feng thought of what had happened in Yanjing and said heavily, "Blame me for not protecting them. I can hardly think of it without blaming myself..."
"Don't take it so hard, Guard Bai. The Jin man who killed Mengrong is dead at her grave, so that debt is paid. We still haven't found who killed Xilan."
"You've done enough, Youqi Jushi. His Highness had the grave prepared long ago. I'll fetch men to carry the coffins over."
"I'll go with you."
Kujue put in, "I'll give a hand too."
The three of them had barely started out when they met Matron Zou coming toward them.
The moment she saw Youqi Jushi her nose stung and her eyes reddened. She came up and took her hand. "I'm so glad to see you alive and back. Now the prince can finally be at ease."
"Matron... I... I didn't look after Mengrong properly. Will you blame me?"

Matron Zou let go of her hand, took out a handkerchief, and dabbed the tears from the corners of her eyes. "Ah, everyone has their fate. This is no fault of yours. You meant well. Blame the times we live in. You've suffered enough yourself. Things will go better from here. All I ask now is that you and the prince walk your road in peace."
She looked around. "Where is the prince? Is he in the house?"
Qianli Xun explained, "The young Jin prince admired his boxing and asked him to stay and trade techniques. He promised to let him come home after a year."
"I hope the young prince keeps his word."
"If he dares break it, I'll kill him."

Matron Zou seized her hand again. "Don't you dare! You must keep yourself safe. If anything happened to you, what would the prince do? I believe he'll come back. He's not a man anyone can threaten. You're his weak spot; only while you're safe can he act freely. I think he chose to stay in Jin for a while himself. And even if the Jin wouldn't let him go, with his skills he'd find a way home."

From all that Matron Zou said, Qianli Xun understood how much Shen Jianchen must have suffered in the days when they thought her dead—enough that the matron, for the prince's sake, could not bear the thought of anything happening to her again.
"Matron, come with me to bury Mengrong and Xilan."
Matron Zou's tears poured down. She let go and wiped them again. "They've come home at last. Princess Consort Yi needn't lie in a foreign land any longer."

The prepared grave was at the foot of the hill beyond the bamboo grove. When they arrived, Qianli Xun found wildflowers of every color growing around it. Mengrong could not have asked for better company than flowers.
With Kujue's help, Bai Feng carried the two chests into the waiting grave.

Qianli Xun brought out the spirit money and offerings she had bought on the way, laid them before the tomb, and crouched with Matron Zou to burn the paper money. The two of them sat a while longer, talking to Mengrong, then went back to the bamboo house.

The house was arranged exactly to Qianli Xun's taste: a tea table, a writing desk, and a bamboo bookshelf. Where he had found so many books she could not imagine, but the shelf was full. The inner rooms suited her too, quiet and elegant—with one thing missing: Kuqiao.
She walked through to the outer room just as Bai Feng came in.
"I was about to look for you, and here you are."
"I have something to ask you, Youqi Jushi."
"Say it."

He spoke up boldly. "My marriage to Kuqiao can't wait any longer. I started building the bamboo house before His Highness left for Yanjing, and it's finished. Will you let me fetch Kuqiao and marry her as soon as possible?"
Qianli Xun laughed. "Granted."
He said delightedly, "I'll go bring her over this minute."
"Wait. Come with me to the Zhu Manor to fetch her, and visit my parents while we're there."
"Kuqiao is still at the Chen Manor," he explained.

"Still at the Chen Manor?" She had thought the marriage was dissolved, Chen Haoyu was with Xiangrong, and her servants would have gone back to the Zhu Manor. Kuqiao still at the Chen Manor—was it the elders keeping her, or Chen Haoyu? "Let's go to the Zhu Manor to see my parents first, then on to the Chen Manor..."
When the servants at the Zhu gate saw the young mistress standing there alive, they were so startled and delighted that they forgot to go and announce her to the master and mistress.
She paid them no mind and went straight to her father's courtyard.
Bai Feng did not follow. He waited outside. He could imagine how the Zhu family would be struck speechless with joy at seeing their daughter whole and safe.

Just as he imagined, the tea cup Zhu Xiyan had lifted to his lips fell and shattered on the floor when he saw her. Tears of joy ran down his face, and it was a long moment before he said to a servant, "Go and tell your mistress!"
Qianli Xun knelt. "Father, I've been a bad daughter and worried you so."
He came forward and helped her up. "Alive is all that matters. Alive is all that matters..."
Madam Xiang hurried in, supported by Chen Wenxin and followed by her son Zhu Jingyuan. As she entered the room and saw her daughter in the flesh, she cried, "Shuzhen! Is it you?"
Qianli Xun turned and went to support her. "Mother, it's me. I'm not dead. I'm perfectly well."
Madam Xiang stroked her cheek. "You've lost weight. I always knew my girl wouldn't die—that one day you'd stand in front of me and call me Mother. Ohhh..."
Chen Wenxin wept with joy too and comforted her mother-in-law. "Shuzhen is home. You should be glad, not crying."
Zhu Jingyuan added, "That's right, Mother. Our sister is back safe and sound. We should all be glad. Come, sit and talk with her."
Zhu Xiyan said, "Stop crying. Sit down and talk."

Madam Xiang choked back her tears and sat with her family, helped by her daughter. Each of them said how much they had missed Shuzhen and asked what had happened to her in Jin, and how the news of her death had reached them.
To spare them more pain, Qianli Xun told only what she could safely tell.
When they heard it, all they could do was curse the Jin for their cruelty and tell her never to go north again. For now, the south was safer.

Asked how she had returned safely, she said nothing of Shao Yueting—that was a Shao family secret. She only said Prince Yi had come to Yanjing again and traded for her, and that the Jin had agreed to let him return to Lin'an after a year.
No one spoke. Zhu Xiyan and the others were thinking how deep Prince Yi's feeling for Shuzhen ran; when he came home, there would be no reason to keep the two apart.
Chen Wenxin thought of her brother, who could not forget Shuzhen and had kept Moxiang Courtyard all this time. If he knew she was alive, what would he do?
Bai Feng, waiting outside, grew anxious. How long would Youqi Jushi be with her family? He decided to go to the Chen Manor first with the good news for Kuqiao and bring her straight back.
As he was about to leave, a Zhu servant came to invite him in. "Guard Bai, our mistress is having a family reunion dinner and asks that you dine with us at the Zhu Manor too."
He declined. "No, no. I have errands."
The servant took hold of him and would not let go. "The master says you must stay today. Our young mistress has come home after all this trouble. Share a little of the family's good fortune."
He could not refuse again, so he went in and ate in a place the servants had set aside for him.
After the reunion dinner the Zhu family sat talking together. In the middle of it Chen Haoyu arrived with Kuqiao, Matron Wei, and Xiangrong.
As he reached the door, he heard her voice inside.
"I'll stay with Father and Mother a while. From now on I'll live at the bamboo house, waiting for him to come back."
Chen Haoyu shut his eyes and a few tears squeezed out and ran down. He stepped inside. Every voice stopped; every laugh died.
Zhu Xiyan exchanged glances with the others, and they all rose and went out.
Matron Wei and Kuqiao bowed first to the master and mistress.
Madam Xiang's spirits had lifted and with them her health. She pulled Matron Wei up. "Come and sit in my room a while."
Matron Wei understood and helped her out, following Zhu Xiyan.
Kuqiao tried to go into the inner room, but Chen Wenxin stopped her. "Where are you going?"
"I haven't seen the mistress in over two years. I miss her."
"Not this minute. Bai Feng is at the Zhu Manor; go and talk to him first." She called a maid. "Take Kuqiao to find Bai Feng."
Kuqiao stole a look into the room, then left reluctantly.
Xiangrong had kept her eyes on Chen Haoyu's back as he walked in, and her heart sank.

Chen Wenxin took her hand. "Don't take it to heart. Haoyu had no choice but to end the marriage. He went to Bianliang to fetch her and missed her, then heard Shuzhen was gone. Now she's come back safe and well; they need to say their piece to each other."
Xiangrong put on an unconcerned face. "I understand. Haoyu's heart has always held Shuzhen. If he keeps the words bottled up, he'll make himself ill."
Chen Wenxin glanced at Xiangrong's rounded belly. "Four months along. You shouldn't stand so long. Come to my room and sit and talk with me."
Xiangrong nodded, cast one more look at the room, and went off with her.
Zhu Jingyuan also glanced inside and sighed. "Ah, Shuzhen's luck in love has never been easy. I hope nothing else goes wrong."
With that, he followed Chen Wenxin and Xiangrong out.
When they had all gone, Qianli Xun stood up. The look on Chen Haoyu's face moved her, and she did not know how to speak to him.

He came slowly closer, each step carrying both reproach and unexpected joy. When he was near enough, the tears fell. "Why didn't you come to me first? If Kujue hadn't gone to the Chen Manor for Kuqiao, I'd have been the last to know."
"I meant to go to the Chen Manor after seeing my family. But you came first..."
He could hold back no longer and pulled her into his arms. "Wife, I missed you so..."
She did not return the embrace. "I'm not... not your wife anymore."
He let go slowly. "Prince Yi lied to me. He's so calculating—he took you from me step by step..."
"That's not it. You have him wrong."
"Wrong? You were alive and he played a grieving man to make me believe you were dead. He had an axe to grind!"
"He really thought I was dead then. He was deceived too. It was my new poems reaching Lin'an that told him I was alive, and he hurried to Yanjing to trade for me."
"Trade for me? Is he in Yanjing?"
"Wanyan Chi says he'll let him come back in a year."

Laughter mixed with his tears. "Hah. He's always been shameless—shameless enough to take every chance anyone had to care for you. In Bianliang he knelt and wouldn't get up, and I lost my marriage. Later he quietly sold everything he owned to raise ten million taels. Now he's run off to Yanjing alone and traded himself for you. Shameless, I tell you! So shameless I can't even bring myself to hate him. I don't want to lose you, and I have to lose you. What am I supposed to do?"
"I hear... Xiangrong is carrying your child..."

"Who told you?" His tears turned to complaints again. "He planned it all, of course. If I'd known, I'd have gone to Yanjing to find you. I was a fool to trust Matron Zou and let myself be talked into coming back to Lin'an. One wrong step, and every step after it was wrong."
"Chen Haoyu, we can't change what's done. We have to face it."
He still would not give up. "The emperor who wrote that edict is emperor no longer. It could be voided. If you're willing, we can restore our marriage tomorrow..."
"Can an imperial edict be voided so easily? And even if it could, I'm afraid I... I could never go back..."
"Never go back? What do you mean?"
"I'm going to live in the bamboo house Prince Yi built and wait for him to come home..."

He had heard the same words at the door; hearing them again from her mouth killed his last hope. He thought of their kiss in the prison cell and stared at her through tear-blind eyes. "Answer me honestly. Did you ever feel anything for me?"
"I tried. I wanted us to make a life together, but things went against us. If none of this had happened, I might be carrying your child by now..."
"I asked whether you loved me."
"I... I kept trying..."
"In the prison cell, when you kissed me—was there love in it?"

She remembered that moment. It was the lowest point of her life. Chen Haoyu had stood by her, and she had been moved; she had thought he was the end of her road, that nothing she did with him could be wrong. That was how the kiss had come about.
His eyes were red with weeping, full of fear and longing. A once dissipated young man had been broken by love for her, and she could not bear to wound him again.
"In that moment I... I should have loved you."
That brought a satisfied smile. "I knew you loved me..." He walked out with that love, content and bereft at once.
Qianli Xun said to herself, "Chen Haoyu, thank you for coming into my life, thank you for loving me. Our fate ends here."
